A minimum-balance fee waiver has a cash cost: compare the extra balance with the fees saved

Use four interactive charts to compare avoided account fees, the additional cash needed to qualify and the after-tax interest that cash could earn elsewhere.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare a full-year fee waiver with the extra cash it requires

Interactive planning lab

Annual fees avoided specifically by holding extra cash$180
Assumed annual interest forgone on that extra cash$75
One-year resource difference: hold extra cash less do not add it$105

Original hypothetical twelve-month comparison for the same account and included services. The entered working floor is the lowest closing balance already planned after ordinary transactions, not the average balance or the full emergency fund. Extra cash is the positive difference between the waiver threshold and that floor. Sufficient additional cash is assumed available at the start. Holding it keeps all waiver conditions satisfied for all twelve months and earns no interest in chequing. Without that extra cash, the fee is charged every month unless the existing floor already qualifies. Both choices start with the same extra cash and receive the same monthly household budget equal to the fee. Unspent monthly budget is retained separately at zero return. In the no-addition choice, the starting extra cash earns the selected effective annual return after its own tax and costs and is not used to pay fees. The normal working cash and other household resources are common and excluded. No actual account quote, daily transaction path, missed waiver, transfer delay, overdraft, product rebate, inflation or personal tax calculation is modeled.

On this page

  1. Read the balance condition before multiplying the monthly fee by twelve
  2. Calculate the additional balance rather than charging the whole minimum to the decision
  3. Give both choices the same cash and monthly budget
  4. Treat the retained principal as an asset and the forgone interest as a cost
  5. Use a cash-return hurdle that matches the comparison’s tax and timing assumptions

The central idea

The relevant comparison starts with the extra cash needed above your normal working balance. Keeping that cash remains a household asset, while its forgone earnings affect the cost comparison.

01

Read the balance condition before multiplying the monthly fee by twelve

The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s chequing-account guidance explains that some accounts waive their monthly fee if a minimum balance is maintained. It also warns that falling below the requirement for only one day can trigger a full monthly charge. The applicable account agreement determines the actual condition.

A monthly average is therefore not enough to establish eligibility under a daily minimum rule. A pay deposit later in the month does not change an earlier closing balance. Review payment dates, debit timing and the amount available before each transaction.

This tool assumes the extra-balance choice successfully meets all requirements for twelve months. It does not simulate a particular account’s transactions or certify that a real household will qualify.

02

Calculate the additional balance rather than charging the whole minimum to the decision

Suppose the invented account requires CAD 4,000 and costs CAD 15 each non-qualifying month. The household already plans to keep a minimum working balance of CAD 1,500 after ordinary transactions. The additional cash needed is CAD 2,500.

The CAD 1,500 working floor stays in chequing under both choices. This comparison therefore considers only the extra CAD 2,500. If the household’s actual planned minimum were zero, the full CAD 4,000 would instead be additional. An average balance of CAD 1,500 would not establish the same result as a minimum floor of CAD 1,500.

When the entered working floor already equals or exceeds the requirement, both modeled choices qualify without adding cash. The incremental fees avoided, interest forgone and resource difference all become zero. There is no extra-balance decision to fund.

03

Give both choices the same cash and monthly budget

At the default inputs, both choices begin with CAD 2,500 available in addition to their common working cash. Both also receive CAD 15 each month from the household budget for banking costs.

The extra-balance choice keeps CAD 2,500 in non-interest-bearing chequing. Its fee is waived, so the monthly CAD 15 is retained separately at zero return. After twelve months, the resources shown are CAD 2,500 of principal plus CAD 180 of unspent fee budget: CAD 2,680.

The no-addition choice keeps CAD 2,500 in an alternative cash account at an assumed 3% effective annual return after its tax and costs. Monthly fees use its CAD 15 monthly budget. The original cash is not drawn down to pay those fees. At year-end, principal and interest total CAD 2,575.

Both start with the same resources and receive the same additional household cash. This prevents fee savings from appearing as free money supplied to only one side.

04

Treat the retained principal as an asset and the forgone interest as a cost

The fee waiver avoids CAD 180 over the year. The extra CAD 2,500 could have earned CAD 75 at the assumed 3% return. The modeled resource advantage is CAD 105: CAD 180 less CAD 75.

The CAD 2,500 principal is not spent as a fee. It remains owned by the household. Its location determines which cash uses remain compatible with the waiver and which earnings are forgone.

FCAC’s review of account maintenance fees identifies the same broad trade-off between fee savings, balance requirements and alternative uses of cash. The figures here are independently constructed, with no bank or product recommendation.

05

Use a cash-return hurdle that matches the comparison’s tax and timing assumptions

With a positive additional balance, divide annual fees avoided by that balance to find the break-even effective annual return. The default calculation is CAD 180 ÷ CAD 2,500 = 7.2%. At that return, the alternative earns CAD 180, matching the fee budget retained by the extra-balance choice.

That percentage is a comparison threshold, not interest earned in chequing. The alternative input is already after its assumed tax and costs, so it should not be filled with a headline promotional rate without adjusting for its actual duration and conditions.

The line varies that alternative return. The matrix varies the fee and the extra balance required. A higher fee can make a waiver more valuable while still leaving a different account with a better overall service-and-cost combination. This same-account comparison cannot rank all available accounts.

06

Check the cash calendar and service needs before implementing the result

Cash kept for a waiver may also be available in an emergency, but spending it can cause a later account charge. Record both uses without treating the same dollars as separate reserves. A planned payment must have a funding route compatible with the actual account conditions.

The FCAC savings-account guide notes that transfer timing can vary. The tool assumes the alternative balance can stay invested for a whole year; it does not establish that transfers will arrive before a real bill or minimum-balance test.

For an actual review, compare the services used, all relevant fees, qualification terms and access needs. A lower-cost account may meet those needs without requiring extra cash. A waiver can be valuable, but its arithmetic is only one part of the account choice.
